item.title: North Atlantic response to a quasi-realistic Greenland meltwater forcing in eddy-rich EC-Earth3P-VHR hosing simulations
item.dc:creator: Eneko Martin-Martinez, Eduardo Moreno‐Chamarro, Fraser William Goldsworth, Jin‐Song von Storch, Cristina Arumí‐Planas, Daria V. Kuznetsova, … (+3)
item.description:
Ocean science — matched: ice sheet, Greenland, meltwater, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation
Abstract. The vast majority of studies examining the impact of freshwater from ice sheet melting on the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) use climate models that cannot resolve mesoscale ocean processes and do not include an accurate spatio-temporal distribution of the freshwater forcing. These two factors critically affect the nature of the AMOC response. Our study fills that gap with a set of three hosing experiments performed with the global configurations of the eddy-rich climate model EC-Earth3P-VHR. The model is forced for 21 years with a spatial and monthly distribution of Greenland meltwater fluxes derived from observations, equal to 0.04 Sv on an annual average. Within the first year, we observe a response of reduced salinity in the Greenland and Labrador currents. This is accompanied by an acceleration and a cooling along the currents that lead to a rapid weakening of the AMOC at subpolar latitudes. Around year 7, deep mixing in the Labrador Sea begins to weaken due to as freshwater anomalies accumulate through lateral exchanges with the boundary currents. This shallowing of the mixed layer further weakens the AMOC, resulting in a stronger reduction that reaches also the subtropical latitudes. By the end of the simulation, the AMOC has weakened by almost 3 Sv at subppolar latitudes (i.e. a decrease of around 20 %), with an average relative decrease of 10 % for the whole Northern Hemisphere. The reduction in the AMOC is strong enough for some global climate impacts to emerge, such as the “bipolar seesaw” temperature response.

item.title: Delayed seasonal march of East Asian summer monsoonal rain belt during Heinrich Stadials
item.dc:creator: Jinzhe Zhang, Ting Wei, Chuncheng Guo, Qing You Yan
item.description:
Environmental Research Letters — matched: abrupt change, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation, paleoclimate, climate change
Abstract The timing and duration of monsoon rainfall shape regional hydroclimate, yet their response to abrupt climate change remains poorly constrained. Here, we use 25-km-resolution climate simulations to investigate the seasonal migration of the East Asian summer monsoon rain belt during Heinrich Stadials, periods associated with collapsed Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC). We find that the rain belt migrated northward 18 days later than during interstadials. This delay kept the monsoon front longer over central China, prolonging early-summer rainfall despite an overall weaker monsoon. The delayed migration was linked to later northward advances of the western North Pacific subtropical high and upper-level westerly jet. North Atlantic cooling contributed to these circulation changes through Rossby wave propagation and a weakened land–sea thermal contrast. Our results suggest that abrupt Atlantic changes can reshape both the amount and seasonal timing of East Asian summer rainfall. These findings offer a palaeoclimate perspective on potential changes in monsoon seasonality under future AMOC weakening.

item.title: Overshoot pathways: reversible biophysical change, irreversible socioeconomic impacts
item.dc:creator: Alaa Al Khourdajie, Marina Andrijevic, Edward A. Byers, Minal Pathak, Anna Pirani, Carl‐Friedrich Schleussner, … (+1)
item.description:
Environmental Research Letters — matched: overshoot, irreversible, global warming
Abstract Exceeding global warming of 1.5 °C in the near term is now unavoidable. An overshoot pathway, in which exceedance is followed by decline to or below the threshold through net-negative emissions, is now the only remaining route back to 1.5 °C. Permanent exceedance forecloses the recovery from climate impacts that an overshoot pathway may permit, yet even an overshoot pathway leaves lasting legacies. To characterise the reversibility of temporary overshoot impacts, we propose a three-layer analytical framework distinguishing hazards (with four dimensions: magnitude, duration, rate of exceedance, and rate of decline), biophysical responses (reversible vs persistent change), and socioeconomic outcomes (reversible vs irreversible impact). We introduce the socioeconomic commitment threshold, endogenous to the overshoot trajectory: how much overshoot intensity a system can experience before the losses it accumulates persist after temperatures decline, explained by three mechanisms: non-substitutability, threshold-crossing, and lock-in. A typology linking biophysical persistence with socioeconomic irreversibility illustrates how reversible biophysical change can produce irreversible socioeconomic loss, while persistent biophysical change need not produce irreversible outcomes where adaptive capacity is sufficient. Whether temporary exceedance produces permanent harm is determined primarily by socioeconomic rather than biophysical factors, except where permanent biophysical change exceeds adaptation limits. For systems and communities with low adaptive capacity, overshoot concentrates irreversible legacies even where temperatures subsequently decline, placing equity and justice at the centre of overshoot assessment.

item.title: Can multi-glacier moraine analysis constrain paleoclimate reconstructions? Evidence from 3D glacier modeling in the Cordillera Real, Bolivia
item.dc:creator: Nicolás Acuña Reyes, Léo Martin, Adrien Gilbert, Vincent Jomelli, Antoine Rabatel, Simon Filhol, … (+3)
item.description:
Climate of the Past — matched: glacier, paleoclimate, Holocene
Glacier deposits are used to reconstruct past climate, but the same glacier size can result from different mixes of temperature and snowfall. Using numerical glacier simulations in the Bolivian Andes, we explored how to overcome this ambiguity. We show that combining several neighboring glaciers with independent rainfall records partly resolves it, giving temperatures 0.8°C and 1.3°C lower during the Little Ice Age and Early Holocene (~10,000 years ago), respectively.

item.title: Evaluating the prediction of subgrid eddy kinetic energy from a machine learning model
item.dc:creator: Thomas Wilder, Ranjini Swaminathan, David Storkey, Till Kuhlbrodt
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: Earth system model, Earth system, parameterization, machine learning, neural network
arXiv:2611.06539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Global climate model resolution is still too coarse to fully resolve mesoscale processes, therefore subgrid closures are required to approximate the feedback of eddies onto the resolved flow. With high-resolution datasets now readily available, there has been a rapid growth in the use of machine learning to develop new eddy closures that could help reduce model biases and uncertainty. In this work we employ an offline learning approach with a convolutional neural network to predict subgrid eddy kinetic energy ($KE_e$), laying the initial groundwork for a machine-learned scale-aware GEOMETRIC eddy closure for the UK's Earth System Model. We address the question of whether global parameterizations are needed or if regional closures are sufficient by evaluating a number of neural network models through region and feature ablation experiments. ML parameterization models generalize to unseen regions when their training data share similar feature and target distributions with those regions. Models that fail to generalize incur distributional shift, or employ different filtering scales for the true eddy kinetic energy field. When holding out features, there is improvement among the generalizable ML models, with some feature spaces leading to improvements in some regions but degrading performance in others. Generally, power spectral density of $KE_e$ tend to diverge at small scales, though some feature spaces are able to minimize this divergence. Overall, the best performing model trained on all regions achieves time-mean and anomaly R2 scores of R2$\approx 0.95$ and R2$\approx 0.8 - 0.9$, respectively.

item.title: Quantifying snowmelt contribution to streamflow using ensemble machine learning and remote sensing
item.dc:creator: Maryam Irani, Jila Dehghani, Fatemeh Ghanbari Talouki, Mohammad Roohi
item.description:
Modeling Earth Systems and Environment — matched: snowpack, ensemble, machine learning, remote sensing
Abstract Snowmelt plays a vital role in sustaining river flows and regulating water resources in mountain ecosystems, particularly under changing climatic conditions. This study aims to quantify the contribution of snowmelt to streamflow by estimating snow cover and snow water equivalent (SWE) in the Greater Caucasus Basin of Azerbaijan. MODIS and FLDAS remote sensing products were analyzed using the Random Forest machine learning algorithm, with data processed on the Google Earth Engine (GEE) platform to improve prediction efficiency and accuracy. Results show that Random Forest significantly enhanced snow cover estimation compared to satellite data alone. MODIS and FLDAS observations revealed peak snow cover in December 2023 (1,310 km²) and maximum SWE in February 2023 (23 kg/m²). Over the longer period 2013–2023, the highest snow cover was recorded in 2016 (5,052 km²), while peak SWE occurred in 2019 (188.7 kg/m²). These findings indicate a weakening role of snow in regional runoff regulation and water supply, driven by declining snowfall and streamflow. The study demonstrates the value of machine learning for snowpack monitoring and highlights the need for long-term simulations and expanded ground-based networks to improve prediction of peak flow events in mountain basins.

item.title: The seasonal, polar-amplified climate response to a latent heat transport forcing
item.dc:creator: Po-Chun Chung, Nicole Feldl, Alexandre Audette
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: polar, albedo, sea ice
Abstract Polar amplification is a well-documented phenomenon driven by multiple feedback mechanisms, with latent heat transport (LHT) playing a role that is often underestimated. Although the total atmospheric energy transport into polar regions remains nearly unchanged in warming scenarios, compensating changes in dry static and latent energy transport interact with polar-amplified surface warming: dry static energy transport generally decreases due to a reduction in meridional temperature gradient, while the latent energy transport increases, contributing to polar warming by enhancing moisture. To isolate the impact of LHT changes, we lock the moisture advection in an idealized general circulation model (GCM) and apply it as a forcing. Simulations forced with an increase in LHT, equivalent to that which would be produced by a doubling of CO 2 , consistently demonstrate substantial polar warming, providing a different perspective from the conventional feedback analysis that attributes polar amplification predominantly to the ice-albedo feedback and lapse-rate feedback. The GCM is coupled to a thermodynamic sea ice model, which allows the role of sea ice to be examined by systematically disabling sea ice-LHT interactions. Sea ice loss strongly enhances annual mean polar amplification and wintertime polar warming, and is itself a response to the increase in LHT. We additionally provide a quantitative comparison of different metrics of LHT-induced polar amplification. These findings suggest that diagnostic decompositions, by only quantifying the enhanced LHT into polar regions and neglecting its impact on polar feedbacks, underestimate the role of LHT as a significant driver of polar amplification.

item.title: Shifts in Rossby wave regimes via the change of group velocity with zonal jets
item.dc:creator: Zhixiang Li, Jianhua Lu, Yimin Liu, Tim Woollings
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: polar, reanalysis, ensemble, extreme event
arXiv:2611.05922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evidences show it is questionable to use the trends in Rossby wave phase speed (Cpx) to interpret the relation between the changes of extreme events and westerly jets. We propose, by using 70 years (1954-2023) of ERA5 reanalysis, that the trends in extremes are associated with the shifts of Rossby wave regimes, via the westerly-induced changes in Rossby wave group velocity (Cgx), which are two to three times larger than those in Cpx. We find significant deceleration in the subtropics and polar regions, alongside a salient midlatitude acceleration, of Rossby wave Cgx, especially over the East Asia-Pacific-North America and North Atlantic-Europe sectors. These changes induce robust shifts in spatiotemporal regimes of Rossby waves, from the transient synoptic-scale regime toward the quasi-stationary planetary-scale wave regime where Cgx decelerates, and vice versa. The CESM2 Large Ensemble confirms that the observed pattern over the Eurasia-Pacific-North America sector is a forced response to external forcing, while uncertainties remain over the polar regions and the North Atlantic. We suggest that westerly trends may reshape the regimes of extratropical Rossby wave activity and extreme weather events through the changes in group velocity rather than phase speed of Rossby waves.

item.title: Past and future projected radiative effects from irrigation
item.dc:creator: Amen Al-Yaari, Chris Smith, Yi Yao, Kjetil S. Aas, L. Ruby Leung, Min-Hui Lo, … (+6)
item.description:
Earth System Dynamics — matched: model intercomparison, radiative forcing
In this study, we use historical simulations (1902-2014) from the Irrigation Model Intercomparison Project (IRRMIP) to provide the first multi-model quantification of irrigation-induced effective radiative forcing (ERF). We find that the global multi-model mean ERF is positive but small (~0.023 W m⁻²). This small global signal masks regional heterogeneity: South Asia and West Central Asia show higher positive ERF (~0.23 W m⁻²), whereas East Asia exhibits a negative signal (~ −0.03 W m⁻²).

item.title: A near-real-time monthly dataset of CO2, CH4, and N2O emissions from fossil fuel combustion
item.dc:creator: Hanlin Niu, Jiaying Fu, Miao Huang, Xi Li, Xianhong Meng, Wenping Yuan, … (+1)
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: CO2
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Fuel combustion is the largest source of greenhouse gases, but existing datasets either lag by years or cover CO2 only. We present a monthly dataset of CO2, CH4, and N2O emissions from fuel combustion for 153 countries and entities, by sector and fuel, from 1960 to 2025. Emissions for 2024 and 2025 are predicted from monthly activity indicators. The dataset supports carbon budget tracking, Global Stocktake assessment and near-real-time monitoring of sectoral emissions.

item.title: Early winter underestimated Indian Ocean teleconnections to the Northern extra-tropics in seasonal forecast models
item.dc:creator: Nazimur Rashid Chowdhury, Muhammad Adnan Abid, Fred Kucharski
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: polar, predictability
Abstract There has been increased attention to the Indian Ocean as a source of predictability for the early winter climate over the North Atlantic European (NAE) region in the form of a North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO)-like pattern. Particularly, the October Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) triggers a delayed precipitation response over the Indian Ocean in early winter, which mediates the Rossby wave that propagates to the NAE sector. Seasonal forecast models have been found to be severely underestimating this teleconnection, and finding the underlying causes is crucial to the improvement of the models’ performance. We demonstrate that models lack an adequate December Indian Ocean convective response, both in terms of magnitude and spatial pattern. This misrepresentation of the heating influences the generation of Rossby Wave Source (RWS) along the subtropical jet. Employing a dry linear baroclinic model, we also find that the December upper-tropospheric mean state does not support accurate downstream wave propagation in the forecast models. Particularly, a combination of a stronger subtropical jet and erroneous polar waveguide zonally traps the wave train in the models. Furthermore, our linear model simulations also suggest that this inaccurate downstream wave propagation potentially affects the strengthening of the wave over the North Pacific.

item.title: Extremes, Teleconnections, and Trends in Growing Season Precipitation over the Corn Belt, 1182–2023 CE
item.dc:creator: David W. Stahle, Edward R. Cook, Dorian J. Burnette, Evan R. Larson, Michael C. Stambaugh, Max C.A. Torbenson
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: paleoclimate
Abstract Tree-ring chronologies were used to reconstruct growing-season precipitation for the North American Corn Belt from 1182–2023 CE. The reconstruction explains close to 60% of the variance in instrumental May–July precipitation totals (1901–2014) and reproduces the teleconnections with circulation and surface climate variables detected in the instrumental precipitation data, substantiating the skill of the reconstruction and indicating episodic co-occurrence of drought between major crop production regions of the central United States and Eurasia. The episode with five consecutive years of deficit May through July precipitation totals in the Corn Belt from 1930–1934 during the Dust Bowl drought was exceeded by several uninterrupted droughts reconstructed during the pre-instrumental period. The early 17 th century drought (1627–1639) was the most severe, sustained, and unbroken drought in the reconstruction for at least 600-years and has no analog in the modern instrumental observations. This drought coincided with decadal dryness in China and eastern Europe and provides a paleoclimatic example of simultaneous megadrought in major breadbasket regions of Eurasia and North America. The decade of wetness during the early 21 st century in the instrumental observations appears to have been unmatched for 700-years and may have been enhanced by increased humidity and radiation changes associated with the dramatic intensification of agriculture in the Corn Belt.

item.title: Identifying Snow-Covered Areas from Unoccupied Aerial Systems (UAS) Visible Imagery and Lidar: A Comparison of Methods
item.dc:creator: Mahsa Moradi, Andrew G. Fleming, Adam Hunsaker, Jennifer M. Jacobs
item.description:
The Cryosphere
Visible images from unoccupied aerial systems (UAS) can be used to map snow, especially where snow is shallow and does not last long. We tested several methods for identifying snow-covered areas using UAS images collected in southern New Hampshire, USA. We found that using the full color information gives the most reliable results. We showed how UAS surveys can be planned to create accurate snow cover maps, helping track snow in changing conditions.

item.title: cSINGV v1.0: development and evaluation of a 1.5 km coupled atmosphere–ocean–wave modelling system for the Western Maritime Continent
item.dc:creator: Rajesh Kumar, Claudio Sanchez, Juan Manuel Castillo, Jian-Guo Li, Bijoy Thompson, Pratiman Patel, … (+6)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Weather over Southeast Asia is shaped by complex interactions between the air, ocean, and waves. We developed a high-resolution model that links these processes to better understand and predict rainfall patterns in the region. The results show that ocean–atmosphere interactions improve the representation and prediction of squall events that affect daily life in Singapore and surrounding regions. This work supports more accurate weather forecasting in the region.

item.title: A deep-atmosphere extension in a nonhydrostatic dynamical core: formulation and idealized tests
item.dc:creator: Qitao Cui, Li Dong, Bin Wang
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Many atmospheric models use shallow approximation that work well when the model top is low. As models top now reach higher layers, these approximation need to be relaxed. We develop a deep atmosphere dynamical core(GMCORE), including full deep atmosphere dynamics, and spherical geometry. The tests case with idealized baroclinic waves and tropical cyclones show that the new model reproduces known results and can alter storm trajectory, suggesting value for future high-top and tropical studies.

item.title: An open-source Python framework for the flexible deployment and advanced applications of the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model
item.dc:creator: Xudong Zheng, Dengfeng Liu, Qiuhong Tang, Qiang Li, Haoyu Liao, Hao Wang
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Hydrological models help scientists understand water movement and predict changes in water resources. However, their increasing complexity makes them difficult to use. This study developed an open-source framework to simplify the setup and application of the Variable Infiltration Capacity model. Tests in multiple basins showed that the framework improves efficiency, provides reliable simulations, and supports wider use of hydrological models.
